newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Rio Tinto says NSW coal performance atrocious.
newsitem.headline: Rio Tinto says NSW coal performance atrocious.

text.p: Rio Tinto Plc/Ltd, formerly RTZ-CRA, said on Wednesday its New South Wales coal mines had a long way to go to improve performance levels.

"In my opinion (performance) is atrocious when compared to the metaliferrous industry," Leigh Clifford, chief executive of the Rio Tinto energy arm, told a briefing for analysts and journalists. Rio Tinto earlier announced plans to unify the management of its two New South Wales coal mining subsidiaries, Coal and Allied Industries Ltd and Novacoal Pty Ltd.
Clifford said that given the potential of the New South Wales coal operations, they should be generating profits of between A$75 million and A$100 million a year.
For 1996, the listed Coal and Allied reported a net profit of A$4 million, down from A$42 million the previous year.
Novacoal saw profits dry up in 1996 after earning about A$12 million the previous year.
Clifford said the problem did not lie in markets for coal but rested solely on the performance of the New South Wales assets.
"The market's not the problem, it's the performance of operations," Cifford said.
Analysts said following the briefing it was doubtful the New South Wales operations would show much if any net profit in the current half ending June 30.
Steaming coal prices are currently about US$37.65 a tonne. Coal and Allied produces about 60 percent steaming coal.
Analysts estimate Coal & Allied's production costs, taking into accout mining, port charges rail, washing and royalties, leaving little if any room for margins.
"Their leverage is in productivity and productivity has been very low due to industrial problems," one analyst said.

Clifford outlined a 12-month plan to turn around operations headed by Kim Tronson as managing director of the new management company. Tronson has held senior positions at Novacoal and Kembla Coal and Coke.
In a related move, Coal & Allied managing director Terry O'Reilly would step down and possibly pursue a new role at Novacoal, Clifford said.
Clifford called on coal mining's highly-unionised workforce to work toward improving performance, but indicated changes would be initiated with or without their support.

"Management and investors and employees have tolerated a work environment that has been pretty unsatisfactory," Clifford said. "We're not going to wait around for 12 months waiting for people to make glacial-like changes. It's up to the union movement if they want to be part of it."
Clifford said the operations would not be put up for sale for at least the next 12 months.
He called the combining the management of Rio Tinto's 71 percent-owned Coal & Allied with its 100 percent-owned Novacoal as a "prelude" to other changes in store for the troubled divisions.
The consolidation was forecast by Rio Tinto to save about A$13 million in costs, equating to about US$1 per tonne of coal on a pre-tax basis.
